chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Upon every truth there is a reality, and upon every correct thing there is a light. So whatever is in accordance with the Book of God, take it; and whatever contradicts the Book of God, leave it.'

key_terms.حَقٌّ: Truth, right, that which is genuinely established — both a juridical and metaphysical category in Islamic thought
key_terms.حَقِيقَةٌ: Reality, essence, inner truth — the deeper substantive core that underlies any claim to truth
key_terms.صَوَابٌ: Correctness, what is right and accurate — practical correctness as opposed to mere truth in the abstract
key_terms.كِتَابُ اللَّهِ: The Book of God, i.e. the Quran — cited as the supreme criterion against which all narrations are tested
key_terms.نُورٌ: Light — used metaphorically for divine guidance, correctness, and clarity that emanates from truth

ai.seo_question: How did the Prophet Muhammad instruct Muslims to evaluate hadith according to the Quran?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) transmits a ruling of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) establishing the Quran as the supreme criterion for evaluating hadith. The Prophet teaches that every genuine truth carries an inner reality and every correct statement shines with a light — a metaphysical principle — before giving the practical rule: authenticate narrations by their conformity with the Quran. This tradition was particularly significant for the early Shia community as they navigated a large body of hadith, some of which were fabricated or misattributed, making the Quran an indispensable filter.
